newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Revolt continues over Australian land rights deal.
newsitem.headline: Revolt continues over Australian land rights deal.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Thursday faced a continued revolt from all sides, including his own allies, over his solution for a national row over conflicting land claims by Aborigines and farmers.

Day-long talks between Howard and his special backbench committee on Aboriginal affairs failed to secure its support for his 10-point compromise aimed at settling the row, which farmers and miners say has damaged their billion dollar industries.

Key committee members told reporters afterwards they were still demanding abolition of Aboriginal rights to government land leased to farmers, an option Howard has declared would probably be over-turned by any court challenge and would cost too much in compensation for Aborigines.

And more than 100 film and sports stars, former politicians and other prominent Australians -- including Treasurer Peter Costello's clergyman brother, Tim Costello -- wrote to Howard on Thursday urging him not to abolish native title.

"We ask you to be courageous and not give in to the destructive forces of selfishness, prejudice or ignorance," wrote the group, including Academy Award-winning actor Geoffrey Rush, star of the film Shine, and Booker prize-winning author Peter Carey.
"We believe that this path could lead to the most serious damage to the social fabric of Australian society and to our standing in the international community," the letter said.

The backbench committee has not yet rejected Howard's compromise, which the prime minister says is the fairest option and gives farmers certainty over use of land they have leased and guarantees Aborigines continued access.
But committee members Bill O'Chee and Bob Katter, both National Party politicians from conservative Queensland state, said abolishing Aboriginal rights was the only solution.
Katter, whose state is one of those most affected by potential Aboriginal claims, said native title extinguishment remained "totally and completely" his bottom line.
The National Party, the junior partner in Howard's Liberal-National coalition, has campaigned strongly for native title extinguishment.
Howard late Thursday publicly released details of his 10-point plan for the fist time, although the central elements have been known for some time.
"I believe that this plan offers the one fair, practical response which, and importantly, provides certainty to pastoralists and miners, but respects native title," he said.

The blueprint, which Howard says is negotiable only on minor technical issues, confirms farmers' rights to land they have leased since European settlement began more than 200 years ago, but guarantees Aborigines limited access for traditional purposes.
It also reduces Aboriginal rights to negotiate over development and other uses of land and exempts cities, towns and water catchments from Aboriginal claims.

Native title laws were introduced by the former Labor government three years ago, but became an urgent political issue when the High Court decided last December that land leased to farmers for generations could be liable to Aboriginal claims.
The row between farmers and Aborigines -- and the members of Howard's coalition -- stems from the failure of the court judgement to define exactly what rights Aborigines still had.
